# The Illusion of Progress


[Chelsey Sassine](https://medium.com/@chelseysassine?source=post_page---byline--e921d165f2d6------------------------------------------)


5 min read


·


2 hours ago

*Why faster coding hasn’t meant faster shipping*


Press enter or click to view image in full size


After years of traveling the world to start up units, I took a permanent job at a refinery. For the first time, I stayed long enough to watch the same unit run month after month, and to hear the same question every quarter.


The Head of Operations would walk into the shared engineering office, smirk, and ask the room if we’d figured out the bottleneck yet.


He smirked because he knew the answer. We were an opportunity refiner, buying whatever crude was cheapest and sometimes switching several times a day. One crude would max out a furnace. The next would push a distillation column toward flooding. The bottleneck was never one thing. It moved every time the crude changed.


That didn’t stop him from asking. When every barrel of crude makes money, the biggest lever is running more of them. Process engineers call that throughput: how many barrels the whole plant processes in a day.


Software teams are asking this question right now. Every feature is expected to make money, and AI makes writing code fast, so why isn’t more code reaching production?


## Only one step matters


The answer comes from a process management approach called the Theory of Constraints. It states that a system can only move as fast as its slowest step.


That step is the bottleneck. Speeding up any other step is a waste because the system produces exactly as much as before. The work just piles up in a different place. Removing the bottleneck raises throughput, but only until it hits the next bottleneck. If that step was close behind, the gain is modest.


That’s the outcome I’m seeing on a lot of teams. Writing code was the bottleneck, and now AI can do in minutes what used to take days. But review was often the next bottleneck, and it got slower when coding sped up.


Most teams changed who writes the code without changing anything around it. They plan the way they always have, but they don’t build by hand anymore, and building was how they used to understand the code. That understanding didn’t go away. It moved to review, which is now where they try to win it back. That stings, because most engineers didn’t join the field to become code reviewers.


So the team doubles its PRs and gets a much longer review queue, with almost no extra throughput to show for it. That’s the illusion of progress. Twice the code, twice the PRs, twice the activity, and the only number that matters barely moved.


## Map it before you touch it


Review might not be your team’s bottleneck, though, and the only way to know definitively is to map it. This is called a value stream map.


A great way to do this is to pretend to be the product. Pick a real change, a feature or a PR, and literally follow it through its entire lifecycle, from the moment it was an idea to the moment it reached production. Write down every queue the change sat in, every handoff, every time it got sent back for refinement or rework, and how long it spent at each step.


That last number is residence time. In a plant, it’s how long material stays inside a vessel. For you, it’s how long a change sits at each step, from idea to spec to code to review to production. The step with the highest residence time is usually your bottleneck.


## Remove the bottleneck


Once you’ve found it, there are three moves, in order.


**Stop wasting its time.** This is the heart of Lean, an approach to improvement built around cutting waste. Anything that takes time without adding value is waste, and waste at the bottleneck is the most expensive kind. An hour lost anywhere else is just an hour. An hour lost at the bottleneck is output the whole system never gets back. Every PR that arrives half-finished, or gets sent back for something a linter could have caught, burns that hour.


Using review to figure out what the code does is waste. That understanding belongs upstream, in the design and the spec, before the AI writes a line. When tests check the outcomes the design promised, review can confirm the change does what it should instead of rebuilding how it works line by line.


**Make it consistent.** Human workflows are a lot like that opportunity refinery. Every ticket is a different crude. Some PRs get reviewed in an hour and some sit for three days, and when a step swings that much, the queue grows in ways nobody can explain. This is the core insight of Six Sigma, an approach built around making processes predictable. Averages hide variation, which is the real problem. When engineers watch p99 latency instead of average latency, they’re making a Six Sigma argument without calling it that. Calm the swings at the bottleneck and the queue stops growing, even before the step itself gets any faster.


**Make sure it stays fixed.** Six Sigma runs every improvement through the same loop, DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. Decide what counts as a process defect, like a PR that waits more than a day for its first review. Then look at what those PRs have in common. That pattern tells you what to fix, and what to watch so it stays fixed. Finally, put the process defect rate somewhere visible, with a target and a range, so you know the moment it starts to drift.


## Software is just getting started


Everything in this post comes from Lean Six Sigma, a widely recognized approach to process improvement. Certification comes in levels, named after martial arts belts.


At my first job, earning a green belt was a rite of passage. The company did process design, pilot plants, and technical guidance, so it was full of chemical engineers, with a new class arriving every few months. Each one was told to find a process and improve it.


Almost all of those improvements were small. Not because the engineers weren’t good, but because the company’s processes had been optimized for decades. The big bottlenecks were gone long before any of us showed up. That refinery was no different.


Software is at the other end of that curve. When someone asks if we’ve figured out the bottleneck yet, no one gets to smirk. The big ones are still out there. So go find yours.
